title: Types and Levels of AI
subtopics: Artificial general intelligence as a research concept
Artificial superintelligence as a hypothetical concept
learning_outcomes: Explain types and Levels of AI and connect at least two of its listed subtopics.
Apply the central idea in types and Levels of AI to a small example or select a suitable approach for a stated scenario.
Identify an important assumption, failure mode, risk, or limitation and describe how it should be checked.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study types and Levels of AI within History, Categories, and Approaches to AI. You will connect the syllabus topics below to a small, inspectable example and practice stating what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: AI contains multiple traditions and capability labels. Compare systems by what they do, how they work, and the evidence available—not by hype.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Artificial narrow intelligence describes systems built for bounded tasks. Artificial general intelligence is a research concept, and artificial superintelligence is hypothetical; these labels do not by themselves establish capability or prove that a system exists.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics covered in this lesson

items.title: Artificial narrow intelligence
items.text: Narrow AI is designed for a bounded task or defined family of tasks. Its performance should be judged within the stated scope, inputs, and intended operating conditions.

items.title: Artificial general intelligence as a research concept
items.text: This label refers to broad competence across many kinds of tasks rather than one narrowly specified task. Treat claims about generality as empirical claims about tested capabilities, not as a conclusion from fluent conversation alone.

items.title: Artificial superintelligence as a hypothetical concept
items.text: This is a hypothetical idea about capabilities exceeding human performance across a very broad range of activities. It is not a claim that such a system currently exists.

items.title: Task-specific and general-purpose systems
items.text: This label refers to broad competence across many kinds of tasks rather than one narrowly specified task. Treat claims about generality as empirical claims about tested capabilities, not as a conclusion from fluent conversation alone.

items.title: Capability-based classifications and their limitations
items.text: Capability-based classifications and their limitations is one of the concepts used to reason about types and levels of ai. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Identify what types and levels of ai takes as input and what result or decision it is intended to support. 2. Read the example before running it and predict the output. 3. Run the small example, compare actual and expected output, then change one input or assumption and repeat. 4. Record what the example demonstrates and what it does not demonstrate about a real system.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with the task definition and the inputs available. Make the expected behavior explicit, choose a simple reference point, and inspect both ordinary examples and cases where assumptions may fail. AI contains multiple traditions and capability labels. Compare systems by what they do, how they work, and the evidence available—not by hype.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: If the output differs, check indentation and spelling, confirm you saved the intended file, and compare each input value with the example. If the example runs as expected, do not infer that it proves a trained model works; this snippet is a deterministic teaching aid. Keep sensitive data out of tests.

content_blocks.title: Check before you trust a result
content_blocks.text: This is a small, deterministic teaching example—not a trained AI model or evidence of production performance. Run it with a local Python 3 interpreter; do not paste secrets or private data into experiments.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: Artificial narrow intelligence describes systems built for bounded tasks. Artificial general intelligence is a research concept, and artificial superintelligence is hypothetical; these labels do not by themselves establish capability or prove that a system exists. Next, connect this lesson to its prerequisite or next lesson and carry the same habit forward: define success, test a representative case, inspect failures, and document limitations.

content.task: Try it yourself: take five example systems related to types and levels of ai. Classify each by its task, input, output, and AI approach; justify one ambiguous case and state evidence that would change your classification. The linked practice activity is: AI or Not AI?.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core concept and accurately refer to the source syllabus topics.
Record a prediction and compare it with a reproducible result or a clearly stated manual trace.
Document at least one limitation, safety consideration, or evaluation requirement.
hints: Write down the inputs, expected output, and assumptions before changing the example.
Change only one input or condition and compare the results with your original prediction.
Ask whether the example covers realistic cases, important subgroups, and failure conditions; a toy example does not establish production reliability.
